title: Data Structures & Algorithms
description: How the collections work inside, and the algorithm patterns behind common interview problems.
resumo: HashMap: 16 buckets, load factor 0.75, doubles on resize; buckets over 8 entries become trees. A bad hashCode makes it a list.
PriorityQueue is a min-heap: O(log n) add/poll, O(1) peek; top-k with a heap of size k. Its iteration is not sorted.
Graphs: BFS (queue) for the fewest hops, DFS (recursion/stack) for reachability and cycles — always with a visited set.
Two pointers and sliding windows turn O(n²) scans into O(n) — two pointers need sorted data.
Dynamic programming: cache overlapping subproblems (memoization) or fill a table (tabulation); no recursive computeIfAbsent.
Choose collections by their most frequent operation; `Arrays.asList` is fixed-size.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an interview asks "how does HashMap work inside?" — and in production, a map with a bad key type becomes as slow as a list.

**Concept:** a `HashMap` is an array of buckets (16 by default). The key's `hashCode` is mixed and reduced to a bucket index; entries that collide in one bucket form a linked list. When the map holds more than capacity × load factor (0.75) entries, it doubles the array and redistributes the entries (a resize, O(n) once, amortized). Since Java 8, a bucket with more than 8 entries turns into a red-black tree (when the table has at least 64 buckets), so the worst case for a bucket is O(log n) instead of O(n).

**How it works:** pass an initial capacity when you know the size, to avoid repeated resizes.
examples.interview_question: How does a HashMap handle collisions, and what happens when it grows?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A `hashCode` that returns the same value for every key (or few distinct values). Every entry lands in one bucket and the map degrades to a list — or to a tree only if the keys are `Comparable`. Use `Objects.hash` over the fields that `equals` compares.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** out of a million orders you need the ten largest, or a scheduler must always run the most urgent task next.

**Concept:** a binary heap is a tree stored in an array where each parent is smaller than its children (a min-heap), so the smallest element is always at the top. Adding and removing the top are O(log n); peeking is O(1). Java's `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap; pass a comparator for other orders. For "top k" problems, keep a heap of size k: O(n log k) instead of sorting everything.

**How it works:** with a min-heap of size k, the smallest of the current top k sits on top, ready to be replaced by a bigger element.
examples.interview_question: How would you find the k largest elements of a large collection efficiently?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Iterating or printing a `PriorityQueue` and expecting sorted order. Only the head is guaranteed to be the smallest; the rest of the internal array is in heap order. Use `poll` repeatedly, or sort a copy.

subsections.subtitle: Graphs: BFS and DFS
subsections.description: Exploring connections: shortest hops and full depth.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** which services depend on this one, transitively? How many connections between two users? These are graph questions.

**Concept:** a graph is a set of nodes connected by edges, usually stored as an adjacency list (`Map<Node, List<Node>>`). Breadth-first search (BFS) explores level by level with a queue and finds the shortest path in number of edges. Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible first, with recursion or a stack, and suits reachability, cycle detection and topological order. Both are O(V + E).

**How it works:** both keep a set of visited nodes, so each node is processed once.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between BFS and DFS, and when do you use each?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Traversing without a visited set. On a graph with a cycle (A depends on B, B on A), the search goes around forever — an endless loop or a `StackOverflowError`.

subsections.subtitle: Two Pointers and Sliding Window
subsections.description: Linear-time patterns over arrays and strings.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** many interview problems have an obvious O(n²) answer with two nested loops — and an O(n) one with the right pattern.

**Concept:** with two pointers, two indexes move through the data — from both ends toward the middle, or one behind the other — and each step discards possibilities, so the whole pass is O(n). It works when the data is sorted or the problem has an order to exploit. A sliding window keeps a range [left, right] that grows on the right and shrinks on the left, updating a running value instead of recomputing it.

**How it works:** look for "pairs in a sorted array", "longest/shortest subarray with...", "substring without repeats".
examples.interview_question: How would you find a pair with a given sum in a sorted array in linear time?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Using the two-pointer pair search on unsorted data. Moving a pointer only discards the right candidates because the array is sorted; without that, it misses valid pairs. Sort first, or use a `HashSet` of complements.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a recursive solution is correct but takes minutes for n = 50, because it recomputes the same subproblems millions of times.

**Concept:** dynamic programming applies when a problem breaks into subproblems that repeat. Memoization (top-down) caches each subproblem's result the first time it is computed; tabulation (bottom-up) fills a table from the smallest cases up. Both turn exponential recursion into polynomial time — for Fibonacci, from O(2ⁿ) to O(n).

**How it works:** define the subproblem, its base cases and how it is built from smaller ones; then cache or tabulate.
examples.interview_question: What is dynamic programming, and what is the difference between memoization and tabulation?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Memoizing with `HashMap.computeIfAbsent` and recursing inside the function. The recursive call modifies the map while `computeIfAbsent` is still running, and since Java 9 it throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Check, compute, then put.

subsections.subtitle: Choosing the Right Collection
subsections.description: Matching the structure to the operations you need.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** performance problems and subtle bugs often come from a collection chosen out of habit, not from the algorithm.

**Concept:** pick by the operations you do most. Access by index: `ArrayList`. Lookup by key or "contains": `HashMap` / `HashSet`. Insertion order: `LinkedHashMap` / `LinkedHashSet`. Sorted, ranges, next-after: `TreeMap` / `TreeSet`. Both ends: `ArrayDeque`. Smallest/largest next: `PriorityQueue`. Shared between threads: `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`. Fixed values that never change: `List.of`, `Set.of`, `Map.of`.

**How it works:** expose interfaces (`List`, `Map`) in method signatures, so the implementation can change without affecting callers.
examples.code:
Operation                     ArrayList  LinkedList  HashSet/Map  TreeSet/Map  ArrayDeque
get by index                  O(1)       O(n)        -            -            -
add at end / at the ends      O(1)*      O(1)        -            -            O(1)
contains / get by key         O(n)       O(n)        O(1)**       O(log n)     O(n)
insert/remove in the middle   O(n)       O(n)***     -            -            -
sorted iteration              no         no          no           yes          no
*  amortized   ** average   *** O(1) with an iterator already positioned
examples.interview_question: Which collection would you choose for frequent lookups by key, and which for keeping elements sorted?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: `Arrays.asList` treated as a normal list. It is a fixed-size view over the array: `add` and `remove` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, and writing to it changes the original array. Copy it into an `ArrayList` when you need to change the size.
